title: Why adult acne happens — and what actually helps
excerpt: Breakouts in your 20s, 30s or 40s are common. Here is what drives them and the treatments that work.
author: Dr. Elena Marsh
body:
Acne is often thought of as a teenage problem, but many patients first see us for breakouts in adulthood. Adult acne tends to sit along the jawline, chin and neck, and it can be stubborn, tender and slow to fade.

## What drives adult acne

Most adult acne comes from a combination of factors rather than one single cause:

- Hormonal changes, including around periods, pregnancy or stopping the pill
- Stress, which raises oil production and inflammation
- Heavy or pore-clogging skincare and makeup
- Some medications and supplements

## What actually helps

Over-the-counter products can help mild acne, but if you have had breakouts for more than a few months, or they are leaving marks, it is worth seeing a dermatologist. Prescription creams, oral treatments and procedures such as peels can bring acne under control and reduce scarring.

Most treatments take 6 to 12 weeks to show clear improvement, so a clear plan and regular reviews make a big difference.

## When to book

Book a consultation if your acne is painful, scarring, affecting your confidence, or has not improved with gentle over-the-counter care.

title: The everyday sunscreen guide for Indian skin
excerpt: How much to use, which SPF to pick, and why sunscreen matters for pigmentation as much as sunburn.
author: Dr. Sofia Reyes
body:
Sunscreen is the single most useful product for keeping skin healthy. In a sunny city like Coimbatore, daily sun exposure is one of the biggest triggers for pigmentation, uneven tone and early ageing.

## Choosing a sunscreen

- Pick SPF 30 or higher with broad-spectrum (UVA and UVB) protection
- Gel or fluid textures suit oily and acne-prone skin
- Tinted sunscreens with iron oxides also help protect against visible light, which can worsen melasma

## How to apply it

Use about two finger-lengths for the face and neck, apply it as the last step of your morning routine, and reapply every two to three hours when you are outdoors.

Sunscreen works best alongside shade, hats and avoiding the strongest midday sun.

title: Hair fall: what is normal and when to see a doctor
excerpt: Losing some hair every day is normal. These are the signs that point to something worth checking.
author: Dr. Marcus Hale
body:
It is normal to lose a certain amount of hair each day as part of the natural growth cycle. Hair fall becomes a concern when you notice a clear change — more hair on your pillow, a wider parting, or thinning at the temples or crown.

## Common causes

- Stress, illness or surgery in the previous few months
- Low iron, vitamin D or thyroid problems
- Hormonal and genetic pattern hair loss
- Scalp conditions such as dandruff or psoriasis

## How we assess hair loss

A hair clinic visit usually includes a detailed history, a scalp examination with trichoscopy, and blood tests where needed. Finding the cause matters, because the right treatment depends on it.

Treatment may include correcting deficiencies, medicated scalp care, prescription treatments or PRP therapy.

title: Mole checks: the ABCDE signs to look for
excerpt: A simple guide to checking your own skin, and when a mole needs a closer look by a specialist.
author: Dr. Arjun Mehta
body:
Most moles are harmless, but checking your skin every few months helps you notice changes early. Early detection makes skin cancer much easier to treat.

## The ABCDE guide

- A — Asymmetry: one half looks different from the other
- B — Border: edges that are irregular, blurred or jagged
- C — Colour: several shades or uneven colour
- D — Diameter: larger than about 6 mm
- E — Evolving: any change in size, shape, colour, or new itching or bleeding

## When to get checked

See a dermatologist if a mole matches any of these signs, looks different from your other moles, or a new spot does not heal. A dermoscopy check is quick and painless.

title: Chemical peels explained: what to expect
excerpt: What a medical peel does, who it suits, and how to care for your skin afterwards.
author: Dr. Sofia Reyes
body:
A chemical peel uses a carefully chosen solution to remove the outer layer of dead skin cells. It can brighten dull skin, improve texture, and help with acne, marks and pigmentation.

## What happens during a peel

Your skin is cleansed, the peel is applied for a few minutes, then neutralised or removed. Most people feel mild tingling. The whole visit usually takes around 30 minutes.

## Aftercare

- Expect mild redness or light flaking for a few days
- Use a gentle cleanser and moisturiser
- Wear sunscreen every day and avoid direct sun
- Pause strong actives until your dermatologist says it is fine

A series of peels spaced a few weeks apart usually gives the best results.

title: Calming eczema flares: simple everyday tips
excerpt: Small changes to bathing, moisturising and clothing that can make eczema much easier to live with.
author: Dr. Elena Marsh
body:
Eczema makes the skin barrier weaker, so it loses moisture and reacts more easily. Good daily care can reduce flares and help treatments work better.

## Everyday tips

- Take short, lukewarm baths or showers
- Use a fragrance-free cleanser instead of soap
- Apply a thick moisturiser within three minutes of bathing
- Choose soft cotton clothing and avoid wool next to the skin
- Keep nails short to reduce damage from scratching

## When to see a dermatologist

Book an appointment if flares are frequent, affect your sleep, or the skin looks infected. Prescription treatments can calm flares quickly and keep them under control.
